Hodograph solutions of the dispersionless coupled KdV hierarchies, critical points and the Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation

B. Konopelchenko Affiliation: Dipartimento di Fisica, Universitá di Lecce and Sezione INFN73100 Lecce, Italy    L. Martínez Alonso Affiliation: Departamento de Física Teórica II, Universidad ComplutenseE28040 Madrid, Spain    E. Medina Affiliation: Affiliation: Departamento de Matemáticas, Universidad de CádizE11510 Puerto Real, Cádiz, Spain
Abstract

It is shown that the hodograph solutions of the dispersionless coupled KdV (dcKdV) hierarchies describe critical and degenerate critical points of a scalar function which obeys the Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation. Singular sectors of each dcKdV hierarchy are found to be described by solutions of higher genus dcKdV hierarchies. Concrete solutions exhibiting shock type singularities are presented.

Key words: Integrable systems. Hodograph equations. Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation.

PACS number: 02.30.Ik.

1 Introduction

In the present paper we study hierarchies of hydrodynamical systems describing quasiclassical deformations of hyperelliptic curves [1, 2]

p2=u⁡(λ),u⁡(λ):=λm−∑i=0m−1λi​ui,m≥1.p^{2}=u(\lambda),\quad u(\lambda):=\lambda^{m}-\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\lambda^{i}\,u_{i},\quad m\geq 1. (1)

These hierarchies are of interest for several reasons. First, there are hierarchies of important hydrodynamical type systems among them. For m=1m=1 one has the Burgers-Hopf hierarchy [3, 4] associated with the dispersionless KdV equation ut=32​u​uxu_{t}=\dfrac{3}{2}\,u\,u_{x}. For m=2m=2 it is the hierarchy of higher equations for the 1-layer Benney system (classsical long wave equation)

{ut+u​ux+vx=0vt+(u​v)x=0.\begin{cases}u_{t}+u\,u_{x}+v_{x}=0\\ \\ v_{t}+(u\,v)_{x}=0.\end{cases} (2)

The system (2) and the corresponding hierarchy are quasiclassical limits of the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation and the NLS hierarchy [5]. For m≥3m\geq 3 these hierarchies turn to describe the singular sectors of the above m=1,2m=1,2 hierarchies [1].

Second, all these hierarchies are the dispersionless limits of integrable coupled KdV (cKdV) hierarchies [6]-[8] associated to Schrödinger spectral problems

∂x​xψ=v⁡(λ,x)​ψ,\partial_{xx}\,\psi=v(\lambda,x)\,\psi, (3)

with potentials which are polynomials in the spectral parameter λ\lambda

v⁡(λ,x):=λm−∑i=0m−1λi​vi​(x)m≥1,\quad v(\lambda,x):=\lambda^{m}-\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\lambda^{i}\,v_{i}(x)\,\quad m\geq 1,

The cKdV hierarchies have been studied in [6]-[8], they have bi-Hamiltonian structures and, as a consequence of this property, the dispersionless expansions of their solutions possess interesting features such as the quasi-triviality property [9]-[10]. Moreover, the cKdV hierarchies arise also in the study of the singular sectors of the KdV and AKNS hierarchies [11, 12]. Henceforth we will refer to the hierarchies of hydrodynamical systems associated with the curves (1) for a fixed mm as the mm-th dispersionless coupled KdV (dcKdVm) hierarchies. The Hamiltonian structures of the dcKdVm hierarchies have been studied in [13]. At last, it should be noticed that the dcKdVm hierarchies are closely connected with the higher genus Whitham hierarchies introduced in [14].

In our analysis of the hodograph equations for the dcKdVm hierarchies we use Riemann invariants βi\beta_{i} (roots of the polynomial u⁡(λ)u(\lambda) in (1)) which provide a specially convenient system of coordinates. We show that the dcKdVm hodograph equations have the form

∂Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βi=0,i=1,…,m,\dfrac{\partial W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\beta_{i}}=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m, (4)

where 𝒕=(t1,t2,…)\boldsymbol{t}=(t_{1},t_{2},\ldots) are times of the hierarchy and

Wm​(𝒕,𝜷):=∮γd​λ2​i​π​∑n≥0tn​λn∏i=1m(1−βi/λ).W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}):=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{\sum_{n\geq 0}t_{n}\,\lambda^{n}}{\sqrt{\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1-\beta_{i}/\lambda)}}. (5)

Here γ\gamma denotes a large positively oriented circle |λ|=r|\lambda|=r. Thus, the hodograph solutions of the dcKdVm hierarchies describe critical points of the functions Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}). These functions turn to be very special as they satisfy a well-known system of equations in differential geometry: the Euler-Poisson-Darboux (EPD) equations [15]

2​(βi−βj)​∂2Wm∂βi​∂βj=∂Wm∂βi−∂Wm∂βj.2\,(\beta_{i}-\beta_{j})\,\dfrac{\partial^{2}W_{m}}{\partial\beta_{i}\,\partial\beta_{j}}=\dfrac{\partial W_{m}}{\partial\beta_{i}}-\dfrac{\partial W_{m}}{\partial\beta_{j}}. (6)

The system (6) has also appeared in the theory of the Whitham equations arising in the small dispersion limit of the KdV equations [17]-[19], and in the theory of hydrodynamic chains [20].

We also study the singular sectors ℳmsing\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}} of the spaces of hodograph solutions for the dcKdVm hierarchies. They are given by the points (𝒕,𝜷)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) such that

rank(∂2Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βi​∂βj)<m.\mbox{rank$\Big(\dfrac{\partial^{2}W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\beta_{i}\,\partial\beta_{j}}\Big)<m$}. (7)

The varieties ℳmsing\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}} provide us with special classes of degenerate critical points of the function WmW_{m} within the general theory of critical points developed by V. I. Arnold and others about fourty years ago [23, 24]. The use of equations (4)-(6) simplify drastically the analysis of the structure of these singular sectors. In particular, we prove that there is a nested sequence of subvarieties

ℳmsing⊃ℳm,1sing⊃ℳm,2sing⊃⋯ℳm,qsing⊃⋯,\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}}\supset\mathcal{M}_{m,1}^{\mbox{sing}}\supset\mathcal{M}_{m,2}^{\mbox{sing}}\supset\cdots\mathcal{M}_{m,q}^{\mbox{sing}}\supset\cdots, (8)

which represents subsets of the singular sector ℳmsing\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}} of the dcKdVm hierarchy with increasing singular degree qq, such that each ℳm,qsing\mathcal{M}_{m,q}^{\mbox{sing}} is determined by a class of hodograph solutions of the dcKdVm+2​q{}_{m+2\,q} hierarchy.

The paper is organized as follows. The dcKdVm hierarchies are described in Section 2. Equations (4)-(6) are derived in Section 3. Section 4 deals with the analysis of the singular sectors of the dcKdVm hierarchies in terms of their associated hodograph equations. The relation between singular points of the dcKdVm hodograph equations and solutions of higher dcKdVm+2​q{}_{m+2\,q} hodograph equations is stated in Section 4. Some concrete examples involving shock singularities of the Burgers-Hopf equation and the 1-layer Benney system are presented in Section 5.

2 The dcKdVm hierarchies

Given a positive integer m≥1m\geq 1 we consider the set MmM_{m} of algebraic curves (1). For m=2​g+1m=2\,g+1 (odd case) and m=2​g+2m=2\,g+2 (even case) these curves are, generically, hyperelliptic Riemann surfaces of genus gg. We will denote by 𝒒=(q1,…,qm)\boldsymbol{q}=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{m}) any of the two sets of parameters 𝒖:=(u0,…,um−1)\boldsymbol{u}:=(u_{0},\ldots,u_{m-1}) or 𝜷:=(β1,…,βm)\boldsymbol{\beta}:=(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{m}) which determine the curves (1)

ui=(−1)m−i−1​sm−i​(𝜷),u_{i}=(-1)^{m-i-1}\mathrm{s}_{m-i}(\boldsymbol{\beta}), (10)

where sk\mathrm{s}_{k} are the elementary symmetric polynomials

sk=∑1≤i1<…<ik≤mβi1⋯βik.\mathrm{s}_{k}=\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<\ldots<i_{k}\leq m}\beta_{i_{1}}\cdots\beta_{i_{k}}.

We next introduce the dcKdVm hierarchy as a particular systems of commuting flows

𝒒⁡(𝒕),𝒕:=(x:=t0,t1,t2,…),\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t}),\quad\boldsymbol{t}:=(x:=t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},\ldots),

on MmM_{m}. In order to define these flows we use the set ℒ\mathcal{L} of formal power series

f⁡(z)=∑n=−∞+∞cn​zn,f(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty}\,c_{n}\,z^{n},

where

z:=λ1/2​for m=2​g+1;z:=λ​for m=2​g+2.z:=\lambda^{1/2}\,\,\mbox{for $m=2\,g+1$};\quad z:=\lambda\,\,\mbox{for $m=2\,g+2$}.

For any given m≥1m\geq 1 a distinguished element of ℒ\mathcal{L} is provided by the branch of p=u⁡(λ)p=\sqrt{u(\lambda)} such that as z→∞z\rightarrow\infty has an expansion of the form

{p(z,𝒒)=z2​g+1(1+∑n≥1bn​(𝒒)z2​n),m=2g+1,p(z,𝒒)=zg+1(1+∑n≥1bn​(𝒒)zn),m=2g+2.\begin{cases}p(z,\boldsymbol{q})=z^{2\,g+1}\,\Big(1+\sum_{n\geq 1}\dfrac{b_{n}(\boldsymbol{q})}{z^{2\,n}}\Big),\quad m=2\,g+1,\\ \\ p(z,\boldsymbol{q})=z^{g+1}\,\Big(1+\sum_{n\geq 1}\dfrac{b_{n}(\boldsymbol{q})}{z^{n}}\Big),\quad m=2\,g+2.\end{cases} (11)

We define the following splittings ℒ=ℒ(+,𝒒)​⨁ℒ(−,𝒒)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{(+,\,\boldsymbol{q})}\bigoplus\mathcal{L}_{(-,\,\boldsymbol{q})}

f(+,𝒒)​(z):=(f⁡(z)p⁡(z,𝒒))⊕​p​(z,𝒒),f(−,𝒒)​(z):=(f⁡(z)p⁡(z,𝒒))⊖​p​(z,𝒒),f_{(+,\,\boldsymbol{q})}(z):=\Big(\dfrac{f(z)}{p(z,\boldsymbol{q})}\Big)_{\oplus}\,p(z,\boldsymbol{q}),\quad f_{(-,\,\boldsymbol{q})}(z):=\Big(\dfrac{f(z)}{p(z,\boldsymbol{q})}\Big)_{\ominus}\,p(z,\boldsymbol{q}), (12)

where f⊕f_{\oplus} and f⊖f_{\ominus} stand for the standard projections on positive and strictly negative powers of zz, respectively

f⊕​(z):=∑n=0Ncn​zn,f⊖​(z):=∑n=−∞−1cn​zn.f_{\oplus}(z):=\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_{n}\,z^{n},\quad f_{\ominus}(z):=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{-1}c_{n}\,z^{n}.

The dcKdVm flows 𝒒⁡(𝒕)\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t}) are characterized by the following condition: There exists a family of functions S⁡(z,𝒕,𝒒⁡(𝒕))S(z,\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t})) in ℒ\mathcal{L} satisfying

∂tnS⁡(z,𝒕,𝒒⁡(𝒕))=Ωn​(z,𝒒⁡(𝒕)),n≥0.\partial_{t_{n}}\,S(z,\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t}))=\Omega_{n}(z,\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t})),\quad n\geq 0. (13)

where

Ωn​(z,𝒒):=(λ​(z)n+m/2)(+,𝒒)={(z2​n+2​g+1)(+,𝒒),m=2​g+1(zn+g+1)(+,𝒒),m=2​g+2,n≥0.\Omega_{n}(z,\boldsymbol{q}):=(\lambda(z)^{n+m/2})_{(+,\,\boldsymbol{q})}=\begin{cases}(z^{2\,n+2\,g+1})_{(+,\,\boldsymbol{q})},\quad m=2\,g+1\\ \\ (z^{n+g+1})_{(+,\,\boldsymbol{q})},\quad m=2\,g+2,\end{cases}\quad n\geq 0. (14)

We notice that

Ωn​(z,𝒒)=(λn​R​(λ⁡(z),𝒒))⊕​p.\Omega_{n}(z,\boldsymbol{q})=\Big(\lambda^{n}\,R(\lambda(z),\boldsymbol{q})\Big)_{\oplus}\,p. (15)

where RR is the generating function

R⁡(λ,𝒒):=λmu⁡(λ)=∑n≥0Rn​(𝒒)λn,λ→∞.R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{q}):=\sqrt{\dfrac{\lambda^{m}}{u(\lambda)}}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\dfrac{R_{n}(\boldsymbol{q})}{\lambda^{n}},\quad\lambda\rightarrow\infty. (16)

The coefficients Rn​(𝒒)R_{n}(\boldsymbol{q}) are polynomials in the coordinates 𝒒\boldsymbol{q}, for example

R0=1,R1=12um−1,R2=12um−2+38um−12,…R_{0}=1,\quad R_{1}=\dfrac{1}{2}\,u_{m-1},\quad R_{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\,u_{m-2}+\dfrac{3}{8}\,u_{m-1}^{2},\quad\ldots

Functions SS which satisfy (13) will be referred to as action functions of the dcKdVm hierarchy. This kind of generating functions SS has been already used in the theory of dispersionless integrable systems (see e.g. [14]). It can be proved [1] that (13) is a compatible system of equations for SS. In fact its general solution will be determined in the next section. We notice that for n=0n=0 the equation (13) reads

∂xS⁡(z,𝒕,𝒒⁡(𝒕))=p⁡(z,𝒒⁡(𝒕)),\partial_{x}\,S(z,\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t}))=p(z,\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t})), (17)

so that (13) is equivalent to the system

∂tnp⁡(z,𝒒⁡(t))=∂xΩn​(z,𝒒⁡(𝒕)),n≥0.\partial_{t_{n}}p(z,\boldsymbol{q}(t))=\partial_{x}\,\Omega_{n}(z,\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t})),\quad n\geq 0. (18)

We will henceforth refer to the dcKdVm hierarchy for m=2​g+1m=2\,g+1 and m=2​g+2m=2\,g+2 as the Burgers-Hopf (BHg) and the dispersionless Jaulent-Miodek (dJMg) hierarchies, respectively. Observe that both hierarchies, BHg and dJMg determine deformations of hyperelliptic Riemann surfaces of genus gg. In our work we will always consider an arbitrary but finite number of these flows.

Since u=u⁡(λ⁡(z),𝒒)=p​(z,𝒒)2u=u(\lambda(z),\boldsymbol{q})=p(z,\boldsymbol{q})^{2}, the operator J=J⁡(λ,u)J=J(\lambda,u) defined by

J=\displaystyle J= ∑i=0mλiJi,Jm=2∂x,Ji=−(2ui∂x+ui,x),um:=−1,\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{m}\,\lambda^{i}\,J_{i},\quad J_{m}=2\,\partial_{x},\quad J_{i}=-(2\,u_{i}\,\partial_{x}+u_{i,x}),\quad u_{m}:=-1,

satisfies J​R=0J\,R=0. Then from (18) it follows that

∂nu=J​(λn​R​(λ,𝒖))⊕=−J​(λn​R​(λ,𝒖))⊖,\partial_{n}\,u=J\,\Big(\lambda^{n}\,R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{u})\Big)_{\oplus}=-J\,\Big(\lambda^{n}\,R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{u})\Big)_{\ominus}, (19)

∂nui=∑l−k=i,k≥1JlRn+k(𝒖),i=0,…,m−1.\partial_{n}\,u_{i}=\sum_{l-k=i,\,k\geq 1}J_{l}\,R_{n+k}(\boldsymbol{u}),\quad i=0,\ldots,m-1. (20)

∂tnlog⁡p⁡(z,𝒒)=∂x[(λ​(z)n​R​(λ⁡(z),𝒒))⊕​p]p⁡(z,𝒒),\partial_{t_{n}}\,\log p(z,\boldsymbol{q})=\dfrac{\partial_{x}\,\Big[\Big(\lambda(z)^{n}\,R(\lambda(z),\boldsymbol{q})\Big)_{\oplus}\,p\Big]}{p(z,\boldsymbol{q})},

∂nβi=ωn,i(𝜷)∂xβi,i=1,…,m,\partial_{n}\,\beta_{i}=\omega_{n,i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})\,\partial_{x}\,\beta_{i},\quad i=1,\ldots,m, (21)

where

ωn,i​(𝜷):=(λn​R​(λ,𝜷))⊕|λ=βi.\omega_{n,i}(\boldsymbol{\beta}):=(\lambda^{n}\,R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}))_{\oplus}|_{\lambda=\beta_{i}}. (22)

The systems (21) are the equations of the dcKdVm hierarchy in terms of the coordinates βi\beta_{i}. Observe that we have two dcKdVm hierarchies, BHg and dJMg, which determine deformations of hyperelliptic Riemann surfaces of genus gg. It can be shown [2, 13] that the dcKdVm flows are bi-Hamiltonian systems.

We next present some examples of interesting flows in the dcKdVm hierarchies. The dcKdV1 hierarchy is associated to the curve

p2−u⁡(λ)=0,u⁡(λ)=λ−v,v:=u0=β1.p^{2}-u(\lambda)=0,\quad u(\lambda)=\lambda-v,\quad v:=u_{0}=\beta_{1}.

The corresponding flows are given by

∂tnv=cn​vn​vx,cn:=(2​n+1)!!2n​n!,n≥1,\partial_{t_{n}}\,v=c_{n}\,v^{n}\,v_{x},\quad c_{n}:=\dfrac{(2\,n+1)!!}{2^{n}\,n!},\quad n\geq 1,

and constitute the Burgers-Hopf hierarchy BH0. In particular the t1t_{1}-flow is the Burgers-Hopf equation

∂tv=32​v​vx,\partial_{t}\,v=\dfrac{3}{2}\,v\,v_{x},

which is in turn the dispersionless limit of the KdV equation.

The dcKdV2 (dJM0) hierarchy is associated to the curve

p2−u⁡(λ)=0,u⁡(λ)=λ2−λ​u1−u0=(λ−β1)​(λ−β2),p^{2}-u(\lambda)=0,\quad u(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}-\lambda\,u_{1}-u_{0}=(\lambda-\beta_{1})\,(\lambda-\beta_{2}),
u1=β1+β2,u0=−β1​β2.u_{1}=\beta_{1}+\beta_{2},\quad u_{0}=-\beta_{1}\,\beta_{2}.

The t1t_{1}-flow of this hierarchy is given by the disperssionless Jaulent-Miodek system

{∂t1u0=u0​u1​x+12​u1​u0​x,∂t1u1=u0​x+32​u1​u1​x,\begin{cases}\partial_{t_{1}}\,u_{0}=u_{0}\,u_{1\,x}+\dfrac{1}{2}\,u_{1}\,u_{0\,x},\\ \\ \partial_{t_{1}}\,u_{1}=u_{0\,x}+\dfrac{3}{2}\,u_{1}\,u_{1\,x},\end{cases} (23)

u=−u1,v=u0+u124,u=-u_{1},\quad v=u_{0}+\dfrac{u_{1}^{2}}{4},

becomes the 1-layer Benney system (2). In terms of the Riemann invariants β1\beta_{1} and β2\beta_{2}

u=−(β1+β2),v=(β1−β2)2/4,u=-(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}),\quad v=(\beta_{1}-\beta_{2})^{2}/4,

the system (2) takes the well-known form

{∂t1β1=12​(3​β1+β2)​β1​x,∂t1β2=12​(3​β2+β1)​β2​x.\begin{cases}\partial_{t_{1}}\,\beta_{1}=\dfrac{1}{2}\,(3\,\beta_{1}+\beta_{2})\,\beta_{1\,x},\\ \\ \partial_{t_{1}}\,\beta_{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\,(3\,\beta_{2}+\beta_{1})\,\beta_{2\,x}.\end{cases} (24)

For v>0v>0 the 1-layer Benney system is hyperbolic while for v<0v<0 it is elliptic.

3 Hodograph equations for dcKdVm hierarchies and the Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation

Let us introduce the function

Wm​(𝒕,𝒒):=∮γd​λ2​i​π​U​(λ,𝒕)​R​(λ,𝒒)=∑n≥0tn​Rn+1​(𝒒),W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{q}):=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,U(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t})\,R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{q})=\sum_{n\geq 0}\,t_{n}\,R_{n+1}(\boldsymbol{q}), (26)

where γ\gamma denotes a large positively oriented circle |λ|=r|\lambda|=r , U⁡(λ,𝒕):=∑n≥0tn​λnU(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}):=\sum_{n\geq 0}t_{n}\,\lambda^{n} and R⁡(λ,𝒒)R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{q}) is the function defined in (16).

Theorem 1.

If the functions 𝐪⁡(𝐭)=(q1​(𝐭,…,qm​(𝐭))𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t})=(q_{1}(\boldsymbol{t},\ldots,q_{m}(\boldsymbol{t})) satisfy the system of hodograph equations

∂Wm​(𝒕,𝒒)∂qi=0,i=1,…,m,\dfrac{\partial W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{q})}{\partial q_{i}}=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m, (27)

then 𝐪⁡(𝐭)\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t}) is a solution of the dcKdVm hierarchy.

Proof.

We are going to prove that the function

S⁡(z,𝒕,𝒒⁡(𝒕))=∑n≥0tn​Ωn​(z,𝒒⁡(𝒕))=(U⁡(λ⁡(z),𝒕)​R​(λ⁡(z),𝒒⁡(𝒕)))⊕​p​(z,𝒒⁡(𝒕)),S(z,\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t}))=\sum_{n\geq 0}\,t_{n}\,\Omega_{n}(z,\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t}))=\Big(U(\lambda(z),\boldsymbol{t})\,R(\lambda(z),\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t}))\Big)_{\oplus}\,p(z,\boldsymbol{q}(\boldsymbol{t})), (28)

is an action function for the dcKdVm hierarchy. By differentiating (28) with respect to tnt_{n} we have that

∂nS=Ωn+(U​∂nR)⊕​p+(U​R)⊕​∂np,\partial_{n}\,S=\Omega_{n}+(U\,\partial_{n}\,R)_{\oplus}\,p+(U\,R)_{\oplus}\,\partial_{n}\,p, (29)

We now use the coordinates 𝜷=(β1,…,βm)\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{m}) so that we may take advantage of the identities

∂βip=−12​pλ−βi,∂βiR=12​Rλ−βi.\partial_{\beta_{i}}\,p=-\dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{p}{\lambda-\beta_{i}},\quad\partial_{\beta_{i}}\,R=\dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{R}{\lambda-\beta_{i}}. (30)

Thus we deduce that

(U​∂nR)⊕​p+(U​R)⊕​∂np=12​∑i=1m[(U​Rλ−βi)⊕−(U​R)⊕λ−βi]​p​∂nβi.(U\,\partial_{n}\,R)_{\oplus}\,p+(U\,R)_{\oplus}\,\partial_{n}\,p=\dfrac{1}{2}\,\sum_{i=1}^{m}\,\Big[\Big(\dfrac{U\,R}{\lambda-\beta_{i}}\Big)_{\oplus}-\dfrac{(U\,R)_{\oplus}}{\lambda-\beta_{i}}\Big]\,p\,\partial_{n}\,\beta_{i}. (31)

On the other hand

∂Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βi=12​∮γd​λ2​i​π​U⁡(λ,𝒕)​R​(λ,𝜷)λ−βi=12​∮γd​λ2​i​π​(U⁡(λ,𝒕)​R​(λ,𝜷))⊕λ−βi.\dfrac{\partial W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\beta_{i}}=\dfrac{1}{2}\,\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{U(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t})\,R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\lambda-\beta_{i}}=\dfrac{1}{2}\,\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{(U(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t})\,R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}))_{\oplus}}{\lambda-\beta_{i}}. (32)

Hence the hodograph equations (27) can be written as

(U​R)⊕λ−βi=((U​R)⊕λ−βi)⊕=(U​Rλ−βi)⊕.\dfrac{(U\,R)_{\oplus}}{\lambda-\beta_{i}}=\Big(\dfrac{(U\,R)_{\oplus}}{\lambda-\beta_{i}}\Big)_{\oplus}=\Big(\dfrac{U\,R}{\lambda-\beta_{i}}\Big)_{\oplus}.

Then from (29) and (31) we deduce that ∂nS=Ωn\partial_{n}\,S=\Omega_{n} and therefore the statement follows.

∎

Using (26) we obtain that the hodograph equations (27) can be expressed as

∑n≥0tn∂Rn+1​(𝒒)∂qi=0,i=1,…,m.\sum_{n\geq 0}\,t_{n}\,\dfrac{\partial R_{n+1}(\boldsymbol{q})}{\partial q_{i}}=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m. (34)

Furthermore, from (21), (22) and (33) the hodograph equations (27) can be also written as [1]

∑n≥0tnωn,i(𝜷)=0,i=1,…,m,\sum_{n\geq 0}\,t_{n}\,\omega_{n,i}(\boldsymbol{\beta})=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m, (35)

which represent the hodograph transform for the dcKdVm hierarchy of flows in hydrodynamic form.

Notice also that we may shift the time parameters tn→tn−cnt_{n}\rightarrow t_{n}-c_{n} in (34) to get solutions depending on an arbitrary number of constants.

It is easy to see that the generating function

R⁡(λ,𝜷):=λmu⁡(λ)=λm∏i=1m(λ−βi),R(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}):=\sqrt{\dfrac{\lambda^{m}}{u(\lambda)}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\lambda^{m}}{\prod_{i=1}^{m}(\lambda-\beta_{i})}},

is a symmetric solution of the EPD equation

2​(βi−βj)​∂2R∂βi​∂βj=∂R∂βi−∂R∂βj.2\,(\beta_{i}-\beta_{j})\,\dfrac{\partial^{2}R}{\partial\beta_{i}\,\partial\beta_{j}}=\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial\beta_{i}}-\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial\beta_{j}}. (36)

Consequently, the same property is satisfied by W⁡(𝒕,𝜷)W(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) for all 𝒕\boldsymbol{t}. Thus, we have proved

Theorem 2.

The solutions (𝐭,𝛃)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) of the hodograph equations

∂Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βi=0,i=1,…,m,\dfrac{\partial W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\beta_{i}}=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m, (37)

are the critical points of the solution

Wm​(𝒕,𝜷):=∮γd​λ2​i​π​U⁡(λ,𝒕)∏i=1m(1−βi/λ)W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}):=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{U(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t})}{\sqrt{\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1-\beta_{i}/\lambda)}}

of the EPD equation

2​(βi−βj)​∂2Wm∂βi​∂βj=∂Wm∂βi−∂Wm∂βj.2\,(\beta_{i}-\beta_{j})\,\dfrac{\partial^{2}W_{m}}{\partial\beta_{i}\,\partial\beta_{j}}=\dfrac{\partial W_{m}}{\partial\beta_{i}}-\dfrac{\partial W_{m}}{\partial\beta_{j}}. (38)

Let us denote by ℳm\mathcal{M}_{m} the variety of points (𝒕,𝜷)∈ℂ∞×ℂm(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})\in\mathbb{C}^{\infty}\times\mathbb{C}^{m} which satisfy the hodograph equations (37). From (32) it is clear that for any permutation σ\sigma of {1,…,m}\{1,\ldots,m\} the functions

Fi​(𝒕,𝜷):=∂Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βi,F_{i}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}):=\dfrac{\partial W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\beta_{i}}, (39)

satisfy

Fi​(𝒕,σ⁡(𝜷))=Fσ⁡(i)​(𝒕,𝜷).F_{i}(\boldsymbol{t},\sigma(\boldsymbol{\beta}))=F_{\sigma(i)}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}). (40)

Then, it is clear that ℳm\mathcal{M}_{m} is invariant under the action of the group of permutations

(𝒕,𝜷)∈ℳm⟹(𝒕,σ⁡(𝜷))∈ℳm.(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})\in\mathcal{M}_{m}\Longrightarrow(\boldsymbol{t},\sigma(\boldsymbol{\beta}))\in\mathcal{M}_{m}.

If (𝒕,𝜷)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) is a solution of (37) such that βi≠βj\beta_{i}\neq\beta_{j} for all i≠ji\neq j then it will be called an unreduced solution of (37). In this case the EPD equation (38) implies that

∂2Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βi​∂βj=0,∀i≠j.\dfrac{\partial^{2}W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\beta_{i}\,\partial\beta_{j}}=0,\quad\forall i\neq j. (41)

Given 2≤r≤m2\leq r\leq m, a solution (𝒕,𝜷)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) of (37) such that exactly rr of its components are equal will be called a rr-reduced solution of (37).

The formulation (27) of the hodograph equations for the dcKdVm hierarchies allows us to apply the theory of critical points of functions to analyze the solutions of these hierarchies, while (38) indicates that the functions WmW_{m} are of a very special class.

The EPD equation (38) arose in the study of cyclids [15], where solutions WW of the above form have been found too. Much later it appeared in the theory of Whitham equations describing the small dispersion limit of the KdV equation [17, 19].

We note that hodograph equations of a form close to (27) have been presented in [20] and [22]. Furthermore, linear equations of the EPD type and their connection with hydrodynamic chains have been studied in [21] too.

Finally, we emphasize that the functions WmW_{m} depend on the parameters t1,t2,…t_{1},t_{2},\ldots (times of the hierarchy). Since ”degenerate critical points appear naturally in cases when the functions depend on parameters ” [23, 24], one should expect the existence of families of degenerate critical points for the functions WmW_{m}. Their connection with the singular sectors in the spaces of solutions for dcKdVm will be considered in the next section.

4 Singular sectors of dcKdVm hierarchies

We say that (𝒕,𝜷)∈ℳm(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})\in\mathcal{M}_{m} is a regular point if it is a nondegenerate critical point of the function WmW_{m}. That it is to say, if it satisfies [23, 24]

det​(∂2Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βi​∂βj)≠0.\mbox{det}\Big(\dfrac{\partial^{2}W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\beta_{i}\,\partial\beta_{j}}\Big)\neq 0. (44)

The set of regular points of ℳm\mathcal{M}_{m} will be denoted by ℳmreg\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{reg}} and the points of its complementary set ℳmsing:=ℳm−ℳmreg\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}}:=\mathcal{M}_{m}-\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{reg}}, where the second differential of WmW_{m} is a degenerate quadratic form, will be called singular points. We will also refer to ℳmreg\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{reg}} and ℳmsing\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}} as the regular and singular sectors of the dcKdVm hierarchy. So ℳmsing\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}} describes families of degenerate critical points of the function WmW_{m}. Near a regular point the variety ℳmreg\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{reg}} can be uniquely described as (𝒕,𝜷⁡(𝒕))(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}(\boldsymbol{t})) where 𝜷⁡(𝒕)\boldsymbol{\beta}(\boldsymbol{t}) is a solution of the dcKdVm hierarchy.

The aim of this section is to analyze the structure of ℳmsing\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}} by taking advantage of the special properties of the set of coordinates 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta}.

In general, the singular sectors of dcKdVm hierarchies with m≥2m\geq 2 contain both reduced and unreduced points. For example, the hodograph equations (42) of the dcKdV2 hierarchy have reduced singular points given by (x,t1,t2,t3,β1=β2)(x,t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}) where

72​x​t32=−9​t22+36​t1​t2​t3+(8​t1​t3−3​t22)​9​t22−24​t1​t3,72xt_{3}^{2}=-9t_{2}^{2}+36t_{1}t_{2}t_{3}+(8t_{1}t_{3}-3t_{2}^{2})\sqrt{9t_{2}^{2}-24t_{1}t_{3}},

and

β1=β2=−3​t2+9​t22−24​t1​t312​t3.\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=-\dfrac{3t_{2}+\sqrt{9t_{2}^{2}-24t_{1}t_{3}}}{12t_{3}}.

Furthermore, there are also unreduced singular points (x,t1,t2,t3,β1,β2)(x,t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},\beta_{1},\beta_{2}) determined by the constraint

360​x​t33=−45​t3​t23+180​t1​t32​t2+15​(8​t1​t3−3​t22)​t32​(3​t22−8​t1​t3),360xt_{3}^{3}=-45t_{3}t_{2}^{3}+180t_{1}t_{3}^{2}t_{2}+\sqrt{15}\,(8t_{1}t_{3}-3t_{2}^{2})\,\sqrt{t_{3}^{2}\left(3t_{2}^{2}-8t_{1}t_{3}\right)},

and

β1=−3​t2​t3+15​t32​(3​t22−8​t1​t3)12​t32,β2=−5​t2​t3+15​t32​(3​t22−8​t1​t3)20​t32\beta_{1}\,=\,\frac{-3t_{2}t_{3}+\sqrt{15}\sqrt{t_{3}^{2}\left(3t_{2}^{2}-8t_{1}t_{3}\right)}}{12t_{3}^{2}},\quad\beta_{2}\,=\,-\frac{5t_{2}t_{3}+\sqrt{15}\sqrt{t_{3}^{2}\left(3t_{2}^{2}-8t_{1}t_{3}\right)}}{20t_{3}^{2}}

From (41) it follows at once that

Theorem 3.

Let (𝐭,𝛃)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) be an unreduced solution of the hodograph equations (37), then (𝐭,𝛃)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) is a singular point if and only if at least one of the derivatives

∂2Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βi2,i=1,…,m,\dfrac{\partial^{2}\,W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\,\beta_{i}^{2}},\quad i=1,\ldots,m,

vanishes.

Notice that since the function WmW_{m} satisfies the EPD equation (38) , its partial derivatives at unreduced points (𝒕,𝜷)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})

∂qWm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂β1q1⋯∂βmqm,q:=q1+⋯+qm,\dfrac{\partial^{q}W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\beta_{1}^{q_{1}}\cdots\partial\beta_{m}^{q_{m}}},\quad q:=q_{1}+\cdots+q_{m},

can always be expressed as a linear combination of diagonal derivatives ∂βikiWm\partial_{\beta_{i}}^{k_{i}}W_{m} with ki≤qik_{i}\leq q_{i}. Thus, for each vector 𝒒=(q1,…,qm)∈ℕm\boldsymbol{q}=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{m})\in\mathbb{N}^{m} with at least one qi≥1q_{i}\geq 1 it is natural to introduce an associated subvariety ℳm,𝒒sing\mathcal{M}_{m,\boldsymbol{q}}^{\mbox{sing}} of ℳmsing\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}} defined as the set of unreduced solutions (𝒕,𝜷)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) of the hodograph equations (37) such that

∂kiWm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βiki=0,∀ki≤qi+1.\dfrac{\partial^{k_{i}}\,W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\,\beta_{i}^{k_{i}}}=0,\quad\forall k_{i}\leq q_{i}+1. (45)

In particular, for 𝒒=(0,…,0,q)\boldsymbol{q}=(0,\ldots,0,q) with q≥1q\geq 1 we denote by ℳm,qsing\mathcal{M}_{m,q}^{\mbox{sing}} the subvariety associated to 𝒒=(0,…,0,q)\boldsymbol{q}=(0,\ldots,0,q). That is to say, ℳm,qsing\mathcal{M}_{m,q}^{\mbox{sing}} is the set of solutions (𝒕,𝜷)(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta}) of the hodograph equations (37) such that

∂2Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βm2=∂3Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βm3=…=∂q+1Wm​(𝒕,𝜷)∂βmq+1=0.\dfrac{\partial^{2}\,W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\,\beta_{m}^{2}}=\dfrac{\partial^{3}\,W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\,\beta_{m}^{3}}=\ldots=\dfrac{\partial^{q+1}\,W_{m}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial\,\beta_{m}^{q+1}}=0. (46)

These subvarieties define a nested sequence

ℳmsing⊃ℳm,1sing⊃ℳm,2sing⊃⋯ℳm,qsing⊃⋯,\mathcal{M}_{m}^{\mbox{sing}}\supset\mathcal{M}_{m,1}^{\mbox{sing}}\supset\mathcal{M}_{m,2}^{\mbox{sing}}\supset\cdots\mathcal{M}_{m,q}^{\mbox{sing}}\supset\cdots, (47)

and represent sets of points whose singular degree increases with qq. Moreover, due to the covariance of the functions Fi=∂βiWmF_{i}=\partial_{\beta_{i}}\,W_{m} under permutations there is no need of introducing alternative sequences of the form (46) based on systems of equations corresponding to the remaining coordinates βj\beta_{j} for j≠mj\neq m.

The next result states that the varieties ℳm,qsing\mathcal{M}_{m,q}^{\mbox{sing}} of the dcKdVm hierarchy are closely related to the (2​q+1)(2\,q+1)-reduced solutions of the dcKdVm+2​q{}_{m+2\,q} hierarchy.

Notice that given 2≤r≤m2\leq r\leq m, the hodograph equations for rr-reduced solutions

βm−r+1=βm−r+2=…=βm,\beta_{m-r+1}=\beta_{m-r+2}=\ldots=\beta_{m},

of the dcKdVm hierarchy reduce to the system

Fi(𝒕,𝜷)=0,i=1,…,m−r+1,F_{i}(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m-r+1,

of m−r+1m-r+1 equations for the m−r+1m-r+1 unknowns (β1,…,βm−r+1)(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{m-r+1}). Now we prove

Theorem 4.

If (𝐭,𝛃)∈ℳm,qsing(\boldsymbol{t},\boldsymbol{\beta})\in\mathcal{M}_{m,q}^{\mbox{sing}} where 𝐭=(t0,t1,…)\boldsymbol{t}=(t_{0},t_{1},\ldots) and 𝛃=(β1,…,βm)\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{m}), then if we define

𝒕(m+2​q):=(tq,tq+1,…),𝜷(m+2​q):=(β1,…,βm,βm,…,βm⏞2​q),\boldsymbol{t}^{(m+2\,q)}:=(t_{q},t_{q+1},\ldots),\quad\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m+2\,q)}:=(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{m},\overbrace{\beta_{m},\ldots,\beta_{m}}^{2\,q}),

it follows that (𝐭(m+2​q),𝛃(m+2​q))(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m+2\,q)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m+2\,q)}) is a (2​q+1)(2\,q+1)-reduced solution of the hodograph equations for the dcKdVm+2​q{}_{m+2\,q} hierarchy.

Proof.

To proof this statement we will use superscripts (m)(m) and (m+2​q)(m+2\,q) to distinguish objects corresponding to different hierarchies. By assumption we have that

(𝒕(m),𝜷(m))∈ℳm,qsing.(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})\in\mathcal{M}_{m,q}^{\mbox{sing}}.

Thus, taking (30) into account, we have that (46) can be rewritten as

{Fi(m)(𝒕(m),𝜷(m)):=∮γd​λ2​i​πU(m)​(λ,𝒕(m))​R(m)​(λ,𝜷(m))λ−βi(m)=0,i=1,…,mFm,j(m)(𝒕(m),𝜷(m)):=∮γd​λ2​i​πU(m)​(λ,𝒕(m))​R(m)​(λ,𝜷(m))(λ−βm(m))j=0,j=2,…,q+1.\begin{cases}F_{i}^{(m)}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)}):=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{U^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)})\,R^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})}{\lambda-\beta_{i}^{(m)}}=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m\\ \\ F_{m,j}^{(m)}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)}):=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{U^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)})\,R^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})}{(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{j}}=0,\quad j=2,\ldots,q+1.\end{cases} (48)

Now a (2​q+1)(2\,q+1)-reduced solution of the hodograph equations for the dcKdVm+2​q{}_{m+2\,q} is characterized by

Fi(m+2​q)​(𝒕(m+2​q),𝜷(m+2​q)):=∮γd​λ2​i​π​U(m+2​q)​(λ,𝒕(m+2​q))​R(m+2​q)​(λ,𝜷(m+2​q))λ−βi(m+2​q)=0,F_{i}^{(m+2\,q)}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m+2\,q)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m+2\,q)}):=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{U^{(m+2\,q)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}^{(m+2\,q)})\,R^{(m+2\,q)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m+2\,q)})}{\lambda-\beta_{i}^{(m+2\,q)}}=0, (49)

where i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m. But it is clear that

R(m+2​q)​(λ,𝜷(m+2​q))=λq(λ−βm(m))q​R(m)​(λ,𝜷(m))R^{(m+2\,q)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m+2\,q)})=\dfrac{\lambda^{q}}{(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{q}}\,R^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)}) (50)

Hence if we set

ti(m+2​q):=ti+q(m),i≥0,t^{(m+2\,q)}_{i}:=t^{(m)}_{i+q},\quad i\geq 0,

we have

U(m)​(λ,𝒕(m))=x(m)+λ​t1(m)+⋯+λq−1​tq−1(m)+λq​U(m+2​q)​(λ,𝒕(m+2​q)).U^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)})=x^{(m)}+\lambda\,t_{1}^{(m)}+\cdots+\lambda^{q-1}\,t_{q-1}^{(m)}+\lambda^{q}\,U^{(m+2\,q)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}^{(m+2\,q)}). (51)

Then it follows that

(52)

Furthermore, for any given i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m we have

=∮γd​λ2​i​π​(λ−βm(m))q​U(m)​(λ,𝒕(m))​R(m)​(λ,𝜷(m))(λ−βi(m))​(λ−βm(m))q\displaystyle=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{q}\,U^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)})\,R^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})}{(\lambda-\beta_{i}^{(m)})\,(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{q}}
=∑k=0qc1,k​(𝜷(m))​Ii,k​(𝒕(m),𝜷(m)),\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{q}\,c_{1,k}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})\,I_{i,k}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)}),

and

Fm,j(m)​(𝒕(m),𝜷(m))=∮γd​λ2​i​π​U(m)​(λ,𝒕(m))​R(m)​(λ,𝜷(m))(λ−βm(m))j\displaystyle F_{m,j}^{(m)}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{U^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)})\,R^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})}{(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{j}}
=∮γd​λ2​i​π​(λ−βi(m))​(λ−βm(m))q−j​U(m)​(λ,𝒕(m))​R(m)​(λ,𝜷(m))(λ−βi(m))​(λ−βm(m))q\displaystyle=\oint_{\gamma}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\lambda}{2\,i\,\pi}\,\dfrac{(\lambda-\beta_{i}^{(m)})\,(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{q-j}\,U^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)})\,R^{(m)}(\lambda,\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})}{(\lambda-\beta_{i}^{(m)})\,(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{q}}
=∑k=0q−j+1cj,k(𝜷(m))Ii,k(𝒕(m),𝜷(m)),j=2,…,q+1.\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{q-j+1}\,c_{j,k}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})\,I_{i,k}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)}),\quad j=2,\ldots,q+1.

where the functions cj,k​(𝜷(m))c_{j,k}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)}) are the coefficients of the polynomials

{(λ−βm(m))q=∑k=0qc1​k​(𝜷(m))​λk;(λ−βi(m))(λ−βm(m))q−j=∑k=0q−j+1cj​k(𝜷(m))λk,j=2,…,q+1.\begin{cases}(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{q}=\sum_{k=0}^{q}c_{1k}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})\,\lambda^{k};\\ \\ (\lambda-\beta_{i}^{(m)})\,(\lambda-\beta_{m}^{(m)})^{q-j}=\sum_{k=0}^{q-j+1}c_{jk}(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})\,\lambda^{k},\quad j=2,\ldots,q+1.\end{cases} (53)

and

{Fi(m)​(𝒕(m),𝜷(m))=0,Fm,j(m)(𝒕(m),𝜷(m))=0,j=2,…,q+1,\begin{cases}F_{i}^{(m)}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})=0,\\ \\ F_{m,j}^{(m)}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})=0,\quad j=2,\ldots,q+1,\end{cases}

and, as a consequence, we deduce the following system of qq homogeneous linear equations for the qq functions Ii,k​(𝒕(m),𝜷(m))I_{i,k}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)})

Because of the linear independence of the polynomials (53) these equations are linearly independent and, therefore, all the functions Ii,k​(𝒕(m),𝜷(m))I_{i,k}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(m)},\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(m)}) vanish. It is easy to see that ℳ2,1sing\mathcal{M}_{2,1}^{\mbox{sing}} is given by the sectors 5 and 6. To check the connection between these sectors and the dcKdV4 hierarchy it is enough to set

x(4)=t1,t1(4)=t2,t2(4)=t3,𝜷(4)=(β1,β2,β2,β2),x^{(4)}=t_{1},\quad t_{1}^{(4)}=t_{2},\quad t_{2}^{(4)}=t_{3},\quad\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(4)}=(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{2},\beta_{2}),

and it is immediate to prove that 𝜷(4)​(𝒕(4))\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(4)}(\boldsymbol{t}^{(4)}) verifies the equations of the first flow of the dcKdV4 hierarchy

∂βi∂t1(4)=(βi+12∑k=14βk)∂βi∂x(4),i=1,…,4.\dfrac{\partial\,\beta_{i}}{\partial t_{1}^{(4)}}=\Big(\beta_{i}+\dfrac{1}{2}\,\sum_{k=1}^{4}\beta_{k}\Big)\,\dfrac{\partial\,\beta_{i}}{\partial x^{(4)}},\quad i=1,\ldots,4.
